clue.text: No classical speech from the commons?

definitions.text: No classical speech from the commons?

parts.words: No classical speech from the commons?
parts.note: the everyday tongue of ordinary people, not Latin or Greek, is the language spoken by the common folk

explanation.walkthrough: 'The commons' here means common people, not the House of Commons; the speech is everyday local language as opposed to the classical languages.
explanation.definitionFit: The everyday native language of a region's ordinary people, rather than a learned or literary tongue.

clue.text: See a dry start to October — opening in there for canal boat

indicators.note: the opening is placed inside the letters already built, the word 'there' pointing at them

parts.note: V stands for vide, Latin for 'see', used in references
TT means teetotal, someone who stays dry

indicators.note: the start to a word is its first letter, so take the opening letter of October

parts.note: a pore is a tiny opening in the skin

explanation.surface: A traveller notes a dry beginning to October before spotting a canal boat through a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in there' puts PORE inside V + A + TT + O, between the A and the TT. TT for teetotal is a standard crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A Venetian water-bus, the motor launch that ferries passengers along the canals of Venice.

clue.text: One with rooted objections to current policy?

definitions.text: One with rooted objections to current policy?

parts.words: One with rooted objections to current policy?
parts.note: someone opposed to the status quo at its very roots, with a nod to the Latin radix meaning root

explanation.walkthrough: The word comes from Latin radix, root: such a person wants change from the roots up, and 'rooted' plays on that origin as well as meaning deep-seated.
explanation.definitionFit: A person favouring sweeping political reform, opposing established policy at its foundations.

clue.text: Titled girl's rolling acres captivate man

indicators.note: to captivate is to take captive, so the letters hold the man inside them
rolling suggests the letters of acres tumbling into a new order

parts.note: Sid is a man's name

explanation.surface: A girl with a title has broad farmland that enchants a suitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Titled' means named in a title: she is the heroine of Shakespeare's Troilus and Cressida. 'rolling' gives CRESA; 'captivate' holds the man inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Trojan heroine gives her name to the play Troilus and ___, so she is a girl named in a title.

clue.text: Subsequent parliament arrests family for unconventional views

parts.note: subsequent means coming later

indicators.note: the parliament arrests, that is holds inside it, the word for family

parts.note: the Althing is Iceland's parliament
kin means family

explanation.surface: A later parliament detains a household for holding unorthodox opinions.
explanation.walkthrough: The Althing, Iceland's national assembly, is one of the world's oldest parliaments; 'arrests' means holding the family inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A term for solving problems by approaching them from an unexpected, unconventional angle.

clue.text: Severe criticism of what one does with cradle, say?

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is to be heard spoken rather than spelt

parts.note: a cradle is something you rock: you rock it

explanation.surface: A rebuke aimed at the way someone handles a baby's cradle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' shows that the words 'rock it', what you do to a cradle, are spoken aloud. To get a rocket is British slang for being told off severely.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a rocket is a sharp reprimand, a dressing-down from a boss.

clue.text: From cliff, draw lake in light shade

indicators.note: to draw is to pull out, so the lake is drawn out of the cliff

parts.note: a bluff is a steep cliff or headland
L is the standard abbreviation for lake on maps

explanation.surface: An artist sketches a lake from a clifftop, using a pale colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw' looks like the artist's verb but means pull out: L is taken out of BLUFF.
explanation.definitionFit: A pale yellowish-brown colour, like undyed leather.

clue.text: Lose nerve, as alcoholic might have?

definitions.meaning: to back out of something through fear, British slang
a heavy drinker might well have a drink container out on the table

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is British slang for losing courage at the last moment; the second reads the phrase literally, a drink always to hand.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for chickening out, and literally a drinker's flask set out ready, both fitting the phrase.

clue.text: Amorous behaviour is to rise, accepted by rival

indicators.note: the rival accepts, that is takes in, the other letters

parts.note: a foe is an opponent or rival

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the words is and to are read upwards, from bottom to top

explanation.surface: Flirtatious conduct prompts a rival to stand up and accept the challenge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rise' reads upwards in this down entry, giving OTSI; 'accepted by' places it within the rival.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing secretly with a partner's feet under a table, a flirtatious game.

clue.text: Gable in block one metre short

indicators.note: short means lacking, so the word for block goes without the letters for one and metre

parts.note: an impediment is a block or obstruction
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A gable on an apartment block falls one metre short of its planned height.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' takes I and M from the front of IMPEDIMENT. 'block' looks like a building, but it means obstruction.
explanation.definitionFit: The triangular upper section over the front of a classical building, the equivalent of a gable end.

clue.text: Cloth adds great weight to bed

parts.note: a cot is a small bed
a ton is a great weight

explanation.surface: Heaping cloth onto a bed adds a lot to its weight.
explanation.definitionFit: A woven fabric made from the soft fibre of a plant grown in warm climates.

clue.text: Rapid current's descent

definitions.meaning: a fast-flowing channel of water, as in a mill-stream
descent in the sense of lineage or ancestry, a people or ethnic group

explanation.walkthrough: 'descent' looks like a downhill run continuing the current, but it means ancestry.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong current of water in a channel, and a group of people sharing ancestry.

clue.text: Breton, say, will bring a number of items to part of England shortly

indicators.note: shortly means cut short, so the county loses its final letter

parts.note: Surrey is a county in south-east England
a list is a number of items set down one after another

explanation.surface: A man from Brittany brings goods to sell in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: André Breton founded the Surrealist movement, so 'Breton' is a person, not someone from Brittany. SURREY is a county south of London; 'shortly' drops its Y.
explanation.definitionFit: André Breton wrote the movement's manifesto, making him an example of an artist of that school.

clue.text: Its martyrs' fate reversed: taken by water

definitions.note: the clue points at a place known for its martyrs, so the definition names that place

indicators.note: reversed means the word for fate is read backwards

parts.note: lot means fate or destiny
a puddle is a small pool of water

explanation.surface: Some martyrs saw their fortunes turned around and were carried off by water.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tolpuddle Martyrs were Dorset farm labourers transported to Australia in 1834 for forming a trade union, so the place is defined by its martyrs. 'reversed' turns LOT into TOL; 'taken by' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dorset village famous for the six labourers deported for forming a union, remembered as its martyrs.

clue.text: Pressing to limit a deduction from wages when taxing

indicators.note: to limit is to enclose within bounds, so the deduction is held inside the word for pressing

parts.note: pushing is pressing
NI is National Insurance, a deduction from wages in the UK

explanation.surface: A tax on pay is pressing hard on workers when deductions mount.
explanation.walkthrough: National Insurance is a British social-security contribution taken from pay packets; 'to limit' encloses it. 'taxing' looks like a tax word but means demanding.
explanation.definitionFit: Demanding and exhausting, as a gruelling schedule wears a person down.

clue.text: Inventor that's illustrious left to the last

indicators.note: the letter for left is shifted along to the final position of the word

parts.note: noble means illustrious or distinguished

explanation.surface: An inventor is so distinguished that he is saved till the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to the last' moves the L of NOBLE to the end. Alfred Nobel invented dynamite and founded the prizes.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Nobel, the Swedish chemist who invented dynamite and endowed the prizes.

clue.text: Duke ran castle badly

indicators.note: badly suggests the letters of ran and castle are jumbled into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A nobleman made a poor job of managing his castle.
explanation.walkthrough: John of Gaunt, Duke of Lancaster, is the best known holder of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: A ducal title held by English royalty, as in John of Gaunt, the duke of that name.

clue.text: Most difficult mountain, but succeeded making the top

indicators.note: in a down clue the letter goes at the top, placed above the mountain

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded, used in genealogies
Everest is the world's highest mountain

explanation.surface: Climbers on the hardest peak nonetheless succeeded in reaching the summit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making the top' puts S above EVEREST in this down clue; 'top' looks like the summit, but it is the head of the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Superlative of 'harsh' or 'demanding': the most testing or rigorous.

clue.text: Have view of old tree

parts.note: a pine is a tree

explanation.surface: Someone enjoys looking out at an ancient tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'view' looks like a sight to see, but here it is an opinion.
explanation.definitionFit: To hold or state an opinion on a matter.

clue.text: Cask full of oxygen always needed for spacecraft

indicators.note: the cask is full of the oxygen symbol, holding it inside

parts.note: a pin is a small cask holding about four and a half gallons
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
e'er, a poetic form of ever, means always

explanation.surface: A tank kept full of oxygen is always essential aboard a spacecraft.
explanation.walkthrough: A pin is an old cask measure, half a firkin. The NASA probes of this name explored the outer planets.
explanation.definitionFit: The name of a series of American space probes, the first to reach Jupiter and Saturn.

clue.text: Clan leader had murderer and thief ordered to be imprisoned

indicators.note: the rearranged thief is locked up inside the murderer

parts.note: Cain, who killed his brother Abel, is the Bible's first murderer

indicators.note: ordered means the letters of thief are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A clan chief ordered a killer and a robber to be locked away.
explanation.walkthrough: Cain, who slew Abel, is crosswords' stock murderer. 'ordered' gives HIEFT; 'to be imprisoned' locks it up inside him.
explanation.definitionFit: The head of a Scottish clan or of a tribe.

clue.text: From battle site an e-mail goes astray

indicators.note: something that goes astray wanders off course, so the letters of an and e-mail are scattered

explanation.surface: A message sent from a battlefield fails to arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: El Alamein in Egypt was the site of two decisive Second World War battles in 1942.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in northern Egypt where Montgomery's Eighth Army defeated Rommel in 1942.

clue.text: Churchman whose moves cut across the rank and file

definitions.text: Churchman whose moves cut across the rank and file

parts.words: Churchman whose moves cut across the rank and file
parts.note: a chess piece named after a senior cleric travels diagonally, cutting across the board's ranks and files

explanation.walkthrough: In chess, ranks are rows and files are columns; the piece shaped like a mitre moves only diagonally. 'Rank and file' looks like ordinary people.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior clergyman, and also the chess piece moving diagonally across the board.

clue.text: Study to gain knowledge and moral insight

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
science originally meant knowledge, from Latin scientia

explanation.surface: Learning brings both wisdom and ethical understanding.
explanation.walkthrough: CON for study is an old word, as in conning one's lines.
explanation.definitionFit: The inner sense of right and wrong that guides a person's behaviour.

clue.text: Priest covering half don Quixote's country

indicators.note: half means take the first half of the region's name, its opening four letters

parts.note: Don Quixote came from La Mancha, a region of central Spain

explanation.surface: A clergyman's jurisdiction covers half the homeland of Cervantes' knight.
explanation.walkthrough: Cervantes' hero is 'the man of La Mancha'; its first half gives the Tibetan priest. 'covering' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: A Buddhist monk or spiritual teacher in Tibet.

clue.text: Obsession as female: I set off to get husband

indicators.note: off means the letters of I set are knocked out of place and rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman sets off determined to land a husband, a real obsession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' turns I SET into ETIS, placed between F and H.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixation or compulsive preoccupation with something.

clue.text: Working, to all intents and purposes

definitions.meaning: operative, in force, as a rule that applies
virtually, in practice if not in name

explanation.definitionFit: A law can be operative, and a thing can be so in practice: the phrase covers both.

clue.text: Clubs with jazz music and rock

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
rag, short for ragtime, is an early jazz style

explanation.surface: Nightclubs playing jazz and rock music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rock' looks like a music style alongside jazz, but it is the definition, a crag being a rocky outcrop.
explanation.definitionFit: A steep rugged outcrop of stone.

clue.text: Pianist's assistant has exciting work

definitions.meaning: someone at a recital who flips the sheet music over for the performer
a gripping book that keeps the reader hooked

explanation.walkthrough: One sense is a person who flips sheets for a performer; the other is a thriller you cannot put down.
explanation.definitionFit: A helper who turns sheet music for a performer, and a compelling novel readers race through.
